title: Introduction to Agents
subtitle: Distinguish adaptive action from a fixed workflow
summary: Pip’s museum guide sends visitors toward a closed gallery. A script would keep going; an agent can observe the closure and revise its plan. Pip gives the guide current information, bounded tools, and a clear limit on what it may decide.

concepts.title: Agent
concepts.body: Pip’s museum guide finds the next gallery closed. An agent interprets inputs, reasons over context, and chooses actions toward a goal. Unlike a fixed script, it can use that observation to revise the route. Pip tests the adaptation and limits its authority before letting visitors rely on it.

concepts.title: Pretraining
concepts.body: Pip’s guide recognizes a visitor’s refund request. Pretraining supplies broad language and world patterns, structured generation, context use, and multimodal capabilities. It does not establish this ticket’s current eligibility. Pip retrieves the purchase record before the guide answers.

concepts.title: Tool use
concepts.body: Pip asks how many exhibition tickets remain. The guide calls a stock tool instead of trusting remembered information. Tools reach outside model weights, but bring permissions, failures, latency, and data contracts. Pip checks the returned quantity and handles unavailable results explicitly.

concepts.title: Agent types
concepts.body: Pip first lets the guide explain museum policy. A bounded business-task agent can also prepare an authorized return label; conversational and autonomous agents have different initiative. That extra action needs permissions and result handling. Pip sets human involvement, context, and acceptable failure for the actual role.

misconceptions.claim: Agent is provided automatically by a more capable model.
misconceptions.correction: An autonomous agent interprets inputs, reasons over context, chooses actions, and interacts with an environment toward a goal. Unlike a fixed script, it can adapt to ambiguous situations, but its autonomy makes boundaries and evaluation necessary.

misconceptions.claim: Pretraining removes the need for evaluation or human judgment.
misconceptions.correction: Large pretrained generative models learn broad language and world patterns before being adapted to tasks. Their capabilities include natural-language understanding, structured generation, context use, and multimodal synthesis; pretraining does not guarantee current or correct answers. Evaluation and appropriate oversight remain necessary.

scenario.title: Calendar agent confirmation
scenario.context: A scheduling agent can read calendars but sending an invitation is consequential. The team has limited reviewer time and must avoid double-booking.

options.label: Read, propose, then confirm
options.benefit: Users retain control and see conflicts before an invitation is sent.
options.cost: Adds a turn and reviewer friction.
options.consequence: A conflict is caught at confirmation and becomes an evaluation case.

options.label: Let the agent send directly
options.cost: A mistaken interpretation creates an unwanted commitment.
options.consequence: Support must undo invitations and add a missing ambiguity check.

scenario.debrief: Both choices can fit different constraints. The decision should state stakes, reversibility, evidence, and who owns correction.

quiz.question: A task needs to adapt after each tool result. What makes it an agent loop?
options: It calls a language model exactly once.
It observes the result and chooses the next action toward a goal.
It always follows the same prewritten sequence.
quiz.explanation: An agent combines observation, decision, and action; a single model call does not establish that loop.

quiz.question: A model confidently invents a current inventory count. What is missing?
options: A longer description of the model’s pretraining.
Permission to repeat the same answer more firmly.
A tool that retrieves the authoritative inventory state.
quiz.explanation: Pretraining supplies learned capabilities; it does not provide a live view of a changing system.

quiz.question: When is a fixed workflow a reasonable alternative to an agent?
options: The steps and acceptable inputs are predictable.
The task has ambiguous goals and constantly changing steps.
No one can define what a successful result looks like.
quiz.explanation: Autonomy adds uncertainty and is useful when adaptation is needed, not merely because a model is available.
